Cecil McBee Part II

Bassist and composer Cecil McBee has played a vital role in multiple genres of jazz since 1964. He has recorded with a lengthy list of artists that include Alice Coltrane, Pharoah Sanders, and Charles Lloyd.
He was interviewed on November 20, 2020 via Zoom, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m pleased to have a second session with Cecil McBee about two weeks after our first conversation. Thanks for finding time again. And you mentioned that you still live, your bio clock, you’re still a nighttime person, is that correct?

Oh yeah. You know when you’re in Tokyo, which is 14 hours in advance of your clock, for a couple of weeks and then you return to New York, supposedly back in reverse to what your rhythm would be about. And then you go to California. And then to Texas. So over all these years I managed to function around this time of the day Eastern Time. I’m up about maybe 11, 11:30.
Okay.
And the first thing I do is run to my bass and make sure that I’m okay. Really. I do.
Is that right?

Yeah, that’s my standard for the day. I’ll play a couple of notes because there’s things that I’m working on now that I’ve had a favor to over the years, things are opening up now on the instrument that, you know, that I’m very excited about. So in a way it’s cyclic.

Well I want to get back to that in a while because that sounds really uplifting. I wanted to make a few stops in your life that you had talked about two weeks ago, and first of all a brief question about your upbringing in Oklahoma. You said that the social conditions there were difficult when you were a child and I wonder if you could expand on that.

Well I was raised by my single parent mother. And there were three brothers and two sisters, right? I was number three in the rotation if you will. And I truly, you know, given recent news about Tulsa, Oklahoma, about conditions that took place during the race riots, okay? My mother had, all these years, had related to us that at eight years of age she had to drop out of school because of the loss of both parents in the same year. This was in © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Southern Texas. And so she and her three sisters, elder sisters, she was the youngest of thirteen kids. They moved to Tulsa, and my mother, Alice, was the only one that had children which was of course us. And she — God I hate to say this — it’s very uncomfortable to say this but I never looked at my father in his eyes and said hello. Or who are you or what is this about. He was nowhere to be found. I think my older brothers, they knew him. They never talked about it. She never talked about it. And so she, when I would ask her about her parents she said, as I mentioned before, they passed away, you know, the same year. And that was it. You never really entered that conversation again. But now with the recent information about these Tulsa riots, you know, I think quite frankly she just didn’t want to disturb us because I think I lost my grandparents in that riot. And then, having moved to Tulsa when she was eight years of age so she said, she could not read nor write ‘til the day she died. So any information that she would impart to me about anything was rather limited. See? So the point is we as kids we had to make out on our own with, being young men, your first thought was to help her, to make sure the burden was off her, insofar as survival was concerned. You know it was always live — food etcetera etcetera. So I think my music began when, not that I realized that this could be my responsibility, that is, to take pressure off Mom, given my own individual needs. I built myself a shoeshine box, right? She gave me a couple of bucks and I bought some polish. I made a little piece of cotton material and a brush and I built this thing, right? You could put your foot on top of it and I would shine your shoes. So right to the right of our house were the railroad tracks. Right? A system of about eight tracks that, you know, provided, you know, travel between the west coast and the east coast. On the other side of that was the other side of town. And I built, I took that box, not knowing what the deal was, walked across those tracks and went into that area and started shining shoes. Right? Then I became pretty popular, this little kid. I was about nine or ten, right? Just nothing but cowboys, horses, and saloons. I remember hearing my first western music while I was shining some guy’s boots. And I got into that because it was like there was something rather tender about that music. You know it was usually somebody missing somebody or somebody feeling uncomfortable about something, the parting or whatever. And so I carried that with me for a while, until I began to grow up. I worked there as a salesman three or four years after that and, you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Can I ask you what the going rate was for a shoeshine when you were doing that, and what would you get to maybe get a tip? What would you do?

I wasn’t very good businessman at the time, you know, I would just, you know, expect something. And apparently I did a good job because I’d get 15 to 20 cents, sometimes a quarter. And quite frankly, if I made over a couple of hours, let’s say three or four hours of work, I would take that money back and give it to my mom. See? And that’s what I did. But then I entered a local farmers’ market not far from the path of the saloons and bars. And a gentleman took a liking to me. And I ended up working for him at his fruit stand. And he sold tomatoes. His name was Jim Hill. He sold tomatoes so my job was when the trucks would bring in the tomatoes I would sort the tomatoes out, we called it “culled” the tomatoes. You’d throw the bad ones out and you’d fashion the packaging and you’d put them out front and you would sell them. I ended up being a salesman, etcetera, etcetera. But one day, I’m about maybe ten and a half now. One day I’m in the back, facing a truck that had brought in a lot of produce, various assortments of produce now. And something — I found myself in the bottom of a barrel. Somebody picked me up and threw me head first in a garbage barrel. Cursing me. I didn’t know what those words were, but I have a scar on my leg now for that. It was the first event of me suffering some effect that said why in the hell are you here. And Jim stood in the way and told the guy, “Look, leave him alone.” So the guy walked away you know. So I got out of the barrel and dusted myself off. And so that was the beginning of life for me because I’ll tell you even at that early age I felt that really, it occurred to me that I could hurt somebody if they ever did that to me again.
Was Jim, you called him Jim, was he a white man?

Yes. He was a white man. I was in the white part of town. That’s why I got thrown in the barrel, I wasn’t supposed to be there, according to this guy. But now the time had passed, you know, Oklahoma, given, now that hindsight tells me now that it’s a travesty it happened, with the race riots. Oklahoma was a very gentle place exteriorly, exterior to my house. I mean everybody was, no matter where you were, they were cool. Loving and caring people. So with Jim I became very good friends with his son, you know, and I worked there for about four or five years until I think I was 13 or 14 then I went elsewhere. I went, lastly, I would, I mean if there were fruits and vegetables that were not © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
so presentable, I would gather those and take them back home to my mother and my family. Right? So that’s what I did until I discovered my bass.
Were you anxious to get out of town so to speak?

Yes. After that incident and, excuse me, referencing your initial effect of your question, given my neighborhood there was just something about it that was uncomfortable for me. The kids of my age, I felt that I needed to enjoy growing up in another fashion. I had no idea what it was but romantically there was something else out there that would provide comfort as an individual that really by now needed to express themself somehow. I didn’t know what that was but I felt that I needed to be able to speak and express myself, necessary to continue to evolve. So I began thinking of, as a matter of fact a couple of times I walked down to those old tracks, this was the Santa Fe Railroad. I walked down to the tracks. Thank God there was no trains coming, I was standing in the middle of the tracks and looked down at all the way to the end of that conclusion of the track, the two tracks where they’d meet at a point. And I said one day I’m going to go that way. Yeah.

Wow. That’s a marvelous story. I appreciate you sharing it with me. You made a stop in Detroit for a while. And we made note of jam sessions at Alice McLeod’s residence. This is the future Alice Coltrane is that right?
Exactly.
Yeah. Can you describe for us what that was like? What would the tunes be? And was the function of it partly to meet people, to maybe find gigs and just improve yourself?

No. The function of it, mind you I’m the young guy. I’m just there you know. I’m out of the exterior if you will. The function of it was to touch base. The musicians that would gather there each and every Sunday that might be in town or might be at home, but just meet and have a good time playing music. So what? It wasn’t about having a gig or anything like that. Because as I mentioned before on the way to New York, now that I’m out of the Army where I practiced my bass every night until three or four in the morning for two years. You know, why was I there at Alice McLeod’s house? I could play the instrument at least to a certain respectable level. So I’m pretty well employed opposite that experience. I was playing a lot. So one good thing about it was I became, I would become friends with Yusef Lateef, with Elvin Jones, with Paul Chambers, people like that that would be there occasionally. And I would also, with open ears, learn from the masters that provided the world at large with the great music out of Detroit. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
Did you join the military or were you drafted?
I was drafted.

Okay. I believe they had integrated seven or eight years before — I’m sort of guessing on the timeline here, but I wonder what the racial conditions or attitudes were like in the military at that time for you?

Here’s what it was. I am now in college. That’s another story as to how I got there. I still don’t believe how I got there. It was the blessings of God, the Gods of music. But anyway I had, as a clarinetist I had entered college on a clarinet scholarship, right? And the moment I entered the school, you know I was playing with some upperclassmen because I seemed to have a pretty good mind for the music. But I got caught up in that and also I met this wonderful lady who was three years my senior. I was a freshman, she was a senior, and so I dropped my scholarship as a young kid. You know now out of that area where I grew up, man I was having a good time. But it turns out my scholarship would provide, you know, the expenses for the school. So I had to drop out of school for a month, work, and then return with money for the next semester. And then drop out of the school for year where I ended up in a steel factory carting hot sand from steel and you know, and all of that. Because really that was quite a mess. But I was earning an education. But it turns out after about three years of that I found no employment at all at the end of my junior year, which was the year that I should have graduated. I was a ;year behind. So that’s when the military, knowing this, they drafted me. Right? So fortunately for me, although I’m now playing the bass, I was still responsible for clarinet activity in the school orchestra etcetera, etcetera. And so upon entering the military I joined the band playing the clarinet. The 158th Army Band out of Ft. Knox, Kentucky. This was America’s largest tank base. Tanks, tanks, tanks forever and ever and ever. And so the wonderful thing about it was now I had a roof over my head, I got paid every month, saving my money, and I’m practicing. I think I might have mentioned before I’m practicing throughout the two years in the basement. So when I got out of the Army and went back to school, and saved my money and went back to school and got my degree, went right to Detroit, see? So that could be an example of how prepared I was because there was nothing to do in the Army but play my instrument.
That’s nice. Yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

When I got to New York, as I mentioned before, you know I was ready to play. I had no idea at the level that I was but the fact that I was feeling, I was experiencing a quality of self worth through my expression you know. That was the greatest thing for me. It wasn’t about who I was playing with or what I was playing, it was that I was now exemplifying those moments in my earlier period where I lived we call it “up on the hill” where I needed to feel something to do something. Now I’m experiencing the reality of that.
Right. You found the end of the railroad track so to speak.
Yeah. I found the groove.

You found the groove. Yeah. Speaking of groove, I wanted to talk a little bit more about, you spoke so eloquently about Paul Chambers and responsibility of notes, and the quarter notes. And I’m trying to form a question here that has something to do with a combination of where you put the quarter notes and what pitches you chooses to play when.
What pitches I use to play —
What pitches you choose to play on what beats and getting from one chord to the next. I don’t really have a question here, Cecil, but —

No I hear you. I hear a question. I’m actually teaching this quite favorably. I’m actually excited about a couple of students I’m teaching, these technique to. You asked me before do I teach them how to play — teach them what to play. I don’t teach them what to play, I give them information as to be capable, to provide that they would be capable in any situation. And see fundamentally the bass player soloing, that is the reward of the effort, the previous efforts, that is to understand that your function, you’re the timekeeper. The pronouncement of that quarter note, given one-two-three-four — the pronouncement of that quarter note is very essential, that not only that it’s pronounced exactly on the beat but that it expands when it’s played only to blend in with the next tone on the second or third beat. Right? So that keeps the time. And even directs the functions of various harmonies that would prevail at the time. The main thing is as a young kid coming along, this is your fundamental reality, that you’re the timekeeper and you know, accented by your choices of qualities of tone. Now qualities of tones reference of course the current scale of the current chord, given your choices of tones as you proceed from situation to situation. I mean really if you know what you’re doing and you understand what the science of that is, that provides, uniquely for the most part, individuality. Because as you © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

choose that tone you are the one that made that decision at that time for that purpose, given how you feel about the moment. Now if you want to, like I did earlier, every now and then infuse something that Paul did, that’s all good as a learning experience, but as you grow and mature then individuality should prevail because you know more of what you’re doing to the extent that you can make unique individual choices. Because see this music that we are excited about in this world is about improvisation of course. Improvisation is about adding something to a given situation, removing something from a given situation, or leaving it — letting it stand entirely. And sometimes that can be in motion or when you’re standing still. You can lay the bar lines down and fashion various progressions that way. So how you, the choice that you make in terms of your reducing something or adding something, you know, as things are progressing, that provides individuality given the extent of your study, which you would provide awareness of really what you’re doing. So this is what I’m teaching these guys you know. It’s not about you’ve got a tune, it’s not what you should play it’s the excitement of choices that you make at the moment as you go from situation to situation. I teach that playing is about a series of crescendos from left to right. It’s about arriving and departing from situations. As you arrive to a situation you are actually leaving a situation simultaneously. There is where the uniqueness of individuality is, the choice that you make at that moment. Leaving and departing and arriving and departing, you see?
Those are some very quotable statements, Cecil.
Oh thank you.

Yes indeed. I will paraphrase them for my saxophone students I think, really beautiful. And I wanted to mention, I forgot to mention last time that I now have two favorite tones from bassists. And you are one, and Buster Williams is the other.

Buster Williams. Oh yeah. Buster is an amazing bass player you know. His tonality, he is the exactness if you will, of what I just talked about, his choices of tones, absent of the tones as they blend in with other tones. He’s really somebody that I highly respect.

Yeah. Excellent. So when you got to New York we talked about you felt pretty good about your musicianship and it sounds to me like you had less of a struggle than a lot of other musicians. I don’t know if you can compare your experience to someone else, but you played from ’69 to ’72 if my facts are correct, both with Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders simultaneously? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
Mostly with Pharoah. I was in Pharoah’s band at the time. Occasionally I’d play a concert with Alice.
Can you describe, first, a recording session with Pharoah Sanders. What did you know beforehand, if anything, when you went to the session? Had you played the music live?

Yeah. Yeah. We, yeah occasionally the music was played live previously, which would upgrade or prepare you for the recording. You know sometimes when you enter the studio you’re unfamiliar with you know any kind of performance of that particular selection. You might have to really focus on the responsibilities that I just explained. But Pharoah was one who — I met Pharoah when I was playing a couple of gigs with Alice Coltrane. And it was like somehow, I forget, but somehow I — oh yeah, I had heard Pharoah’s record called “Karma,” right? And I heard it on the radio so I bought a copy of it, it was one of those vinyl records. And I couldn’t take it off for months because I loved it. It was a vamp that just maintained and maintained and see that’s what Pharoah was about you know. You establish a tonal center from which many things can spring, given various collectives of individuality. But I couldn’t get past the bass player on that record, who was Richard Davis, who is to this day my previous idol, along with Paul Chambers. Richard Davis, the sound of his tone and his quality of tonal pronouncement, which is where I — how do you say — found my initial techniques for teaching the placement of the quarter note was through that record “Karma.” The way he played his notes just blew me away and that’s kind of how I play now, blended in with some techniques of Paul Chambers. And also Richard was one who was — in other areas of improvisation — was one who would pour over the glass, pour over the border of the instrument. He was always one that was like playing other things past what responsibility was. And I liked that because that gave me reason to express who I really was, that is someone that wanted to become more expressive out there in the area that I wasn’t familiar with.
I see.

And the way to do that was to put all those techniques I spoke about before and just go out there and play that referencing where you came from. You see? So that’s how I ended up in Pharoah’s band because that’s what we did — maybe on a B flat 7 we would vamp forever and everybody would be free to play back and forth, across the line, harmonically or whatever. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
Right. I just was listening to some of that kind of thing, and there was a tune, “Prince of Peace”
Yeah.
And the overall quality of it is fairly peaceful but at around ten minutes —
I know what you’re going to say.

You’re talking about things that can spring out of people. And it shocked me and honestly it’s rather frightening until it’s just — I’m wondering if you remember that specifically and do you believe that Pharoah expected the accompanists to go with him?

Absolutely. Absolutely. Now that you have provided assurance that what is taking place currently is secure in terms of its intent to express, it’s all right to go there now. Because you’ve provided that premise from which it comes. See? So in performance it’s okay to go out there because you’ve done so well which causes for you to feel that it’s okay to go out there that you know in leaving where you were, the memory of that prevails. So you can just do what you want you know, and play collectively, everybody’s listening and adhering to the rules of tone placement, of harmonic placement, rhythmic let’s say, what’s the word —
Interaction?

Interaction. Yeah. And so you are out there, you are doing your thing only to return to where you came from or either let it go. For instance, speaking of Pharoah the current bass that I have now, which I’ve had since then, this is 1969. My principal bass, I have one other, I had gone into a store on 42nd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues in New York, but it was a bass shop, to get some strings. And there were three basses on a rack. And the first bass really appealed to me. It had the shape and curves that just were wonderful, past what I had experienced before, just like an upgrade. So I played it and fell in love with it and ended up buying it. Right? And so that was two weeks before we recorded “Thembi.” So in the studio we were going to play this tune, and Pharoah being somewhat unpredictable at times in terms of what he would play, when he would play, and how he would play, you had to go with that. He said, “Hey, look, let McBee play something out front and then we’ll come in at Letter A at my cue.” Right? So I just started playing. And this was a tune called “Love” that to this day in my travels around the world people were very very appreciative of my quality of expression, my quality of thought. And I mean that was like although I had played with other people before that it © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
is said that that’s when the world acknowledged that there’s a new bass player in town, Cecil McBee.
All right.

Overnight I went to my head in my living room and just started playing all my stuff that I practiced. Right? And then when I finished we went into the tune. So that was the thing to do with Pharoah. Either you begin outside of the music and you entered some structure then you left it. And so I was with him for about three years and it was just a wonderful experience.
Was there ever any question how these tunes were going to end? How do you get to the end?
Of course, some tunes were like, of course. By the way now that the melody is played we’ll ritard here and we’ll end there. Of course we would do that.
Yes.

But a lot of the times finding an ending was rather difficult so the tune would continue until you found something, you’d get the hell out of there, but that was all fun you know. Because before what had prevailed was the volume of music that you had played that was wonderful, you know, given the excitement of the audience, but upon ending you couldn’t do anything wrong.
I think I know the answer to this but can I guess that the practice of overdubbing was not employed on these recordings.
Not with Pharoah, no. Ut um. We did that later on when I was with —
Who was that?

Jackie McLean, we did that when things were more or less in line structurally, etcetera, etcetera. You know you would open up. That’s when they had those tapes, you know those big thick tapes. But with Pharoah I don’t recall ever doing that with anything, the things were like from A all the way to Z and past, with fury, either be it in the quietest of the night or the loudest of the center of the city.
Did you ever read reviews on some of these recordings or live gigs with Pharoah where the reviewer called the music “angry?”
Never heard of that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Okay. I’m sort of glad. Because well I think sometimes people associate free jazz, especially during the Civil Rights Movement as if it had to have, as if it were expressing anger.

Well you’ve got to remember, sorry to interrupt, that exterior out there, those who profess that they know what they’re talking about in terms of what the intent of the music is, should kind of like move back a little bit. Because you know if you’re going to consider what we were doing, you know, you are lost buddy, or whoever you are. Because Pharoah’s music was all about peace and happiness. That was what “Karma” was about. [scats] [sings] He said happiness for everyone. And he’d play that vamp forever. That’s what he was about. Even when the music would go off the structure, that was like somebody getting happy with the spirit in church.
That explains it for me.

I can remember when I was about — it was about a year and a half before I began shining shoes. I ended up staying, living with my paternal grandmother. And the moment I entered her home — she had a Bible right here. She set me down on the bed and began reading to me the first passages. I had no idea what was going on. My feet weren’t even touching the floor. But she was like, she called me “Season”. “Season, sit down.” “And Jesus said” etcetera, etcetera. You know. And if I listened well I got a piece of that pound cake out of the pantry. Right? But her church was right next door. You could walk through her side, there was a door on the side of the house, across a little walkway and into a church, right? And I remember sitting there, my legs are still not, my feet are still not touching the floor. She’s to my right, right? And the preacher was preaching to a point of excitement that I got a little afraid. You know it was my first time hearing something at that intensity. And then suddenly my grandmother got the spirit. And she’s on the floor now, and these ladies are fanning her. Fanning her. And the church is still having this celebration of life. And so I thought, I said I mean she was out. You know? So I thought it would be a good idea to get up and go back through the walkway back into the house. And the moment I put my foot on the floor she grabbed me like that. My left hand. “Help me.” Right? And man I’ll tell you, when she grabbed me she was — I felt something. Right? And so that experience is what gave me some reason to believe, to understand more the in depth performances with Pharoah because it was all about that © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
kind of vibe. It’s about the celebration of love and peace and positivity. So I was with him three years and it was absolutely wonderful.

The second line to the melody you were singing goes Peace and happiness — “the creator makes but one demand, peace and happiness through all the land.” And I’m wondering if you feel in this day and age that that’s possible?

Of course. It’s from whence it comes. We had an extreme deviation from that reality. Reality is love and love is true. That’s the message. It’s what causes the manifestation of all things. That’s our nucleus. That’s our soul. It’s always there. It’s a matter of how far you get away from it, which can lead you the wrong way you know. And I think the world at large now, this world of ours, is suffering a major distraction from that premise, from the soul of what America has always been about. I mentioned before about in Oklahoma, the love that I got from the community you know, and you know America, hey, I mean we’re diverse but one of the greater things that we are very, very conscious of and proud of is that there’s a great intense amount of love here, in various forms it takes. It has been distracted.
Wow. Thanks for sharing that.

America, this is a wonderful place, man. Look at what we have here. You know everything that you can possibly imagine creatively and possibilities, you know, are here you know. I think that given other nations that have suffered through passages or situations socially, economically, whatever, for instance look at China. They suffered Japan’s situation. Look at the Greeks, the Italians, etcetera, etcetera. America is now right in the center of a passage. It’s growing up. This situation is causing us to be aware of not only who we are but ourselves individually. It’s a natural unfoldment of things. Every country goes through it. This is a very natural thing. This man came along and said hey, you know, you now have to become aware of who you are and what your intent is through the respect or acknowledgment of that person six feet away from you. What is all that about? This young country, America, is growing up, out of its teenage years. It’s just a natural unfoldment. It all depends on how we handle it.
So on your website I’m going to suggest that you add to your bassist/composer/educator, also philosopher, Cecil.
Oh no, no. No. I just say what I think it is you know, I’m not a philosopher. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Well it was a compliment. So. So over my shoulders I have pictures of a few of my musical heroes including Cannonball Adderley, Lester Young, Count Basie. And I know you worked with Dinah Washington. So the music of these people may be looked at as less spiritual than the music you played with Pharoah Sanders. So I’m wondering how you think of that music in society. What is the role of that music in society?

I don’t think it’s any less spiritual. I think it’s just a different approach. Remember I mentioned earlier that it’s about adding something, taking something away, how you manage those conditions as they flow into — and conceptually these individuals are doing their thing accordingly, more or less effort, more or less intent to express, maybe not a spiritual situation but a statement that references the moment of who they are individually and collectively. As I profess, if you will initially, earlier, it can’t be done the same way. We all, I mentioned, again, that your unique approach to that particular moment is what makes your intent unique and the result unique. So your uniqueness are very inspirational to cause for me or us to not only want to more or less appreciate that, but to find your own individuality so that you can perhaps make a statement as large as they did in your own way. For instance, as a clarinetist, in junior high school, my initial phases of my prowess on the clarinet, given my junior high school band, we were all required to sit in the early evening, about 7:00, this was in Tulsa, in the football stadium. Every student had to be there. Why? We had no idea, right? But in the center of the field, at the 50 yard line was a piano, a bass and a set of drums. Right? So us being kids, you know, middle school, what the hell is this. Let’s get through the thing and go home. Okay? It turns out it was Lester Young. They were — God bless them. When I heard that music, when I first heard it it was like there was something about it that touched me according to how I felt about things. I mean there was something about it that, you know, made me want to feel good and maybe realize something else. How great they were. This was total, you know, an African-American neighborhood. And I can never forget that. That was really the beginning of me wanting to play music down the line once I heard music that was similar to that. You know so —
That’s an amazing story. I’ve had similar experiences but it was on recordings and you’re so touched by something that you’re compelled to go find out more about that.
Yeah. What was it — how did I get into that? © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
Well I had talked about Cannonball and Lester Young, and you were saying that their music was spiritual just in a different way.

Well if it ain’t spiritual don’t play it. If it’s not — you know your spirit is what makes you you know play the instrument. No piano player. So we had a good time. And then a couple of months later we were in the same room. Somebody knocks on the door. And Wesley, my buddy, alto player, who was a star forward for the basketball team, he opened the door and there was this guy in all of this color, you know, and he was about the size of Miles Davis. early October. The window was out. There was a towel to prevent the wind from coming in. I played my first gig with Jimmy “Cry Cry,” with — standing on his head. This was before James Brown. I love it.
And seriously, to this day, Jimmy “Cry Cry” is a great part of Tulsa’s history.

Yeah, the point is, I didn’t make, is that the moment I touched that bass, the first moment I touched that bass I was the new bass player in town ‘cause there were no bass players there. So you know I was tolerated until I could find my way.

Well it wasn’t too long after this episode with Jimmy “Cry Cry” that what’s his name, it jumped off my tongue, I ended up in the jazz club in Tulsa, Oklahoma, which was called Clarence Love’s Lounge. Clarence Love was one of the big band leaders throughout the 20s and early 30s that traveled throughout the southwest along with another local big band headed by — jumped right out of my head now — but it’ll come back to me — but he apparently had reasonable — well Tulsa is not too far north of Houston, not too far south of Kansas City, right? 92 miles east of Oklahoma City. It was right in the heart of Route 66 so there were a lot of musical activity in that area. So apparently I had a decent ear because you know after the year that is the complete year of my junior year in high school I knew all my standard tunes. Well the percussive qualities of the stand-up bass I think are so important, beyond the incorrect notes you might play if you were providing that rhythm for the dancers and so forth, that would have been enough to keep you on the bandstand.

When that feeling occurs I, quite frankly, even at that particular time I would sit at the piano and I would play something that might give me reason to feel more relaxed and more acceptable to a nice sound, and then if that sound pleases me I will try to respond to it with a subsequent sound. And so forth and so forth and so on. And I’ve learned that rather than try to compare that moment with what had prevailed, the uniqueness of it would be that you know write it down at the moment of the situation.
